judge.detail: The answer attributes the weakness to specific soil types (Wehadkee, Roanoke, Augusta) concentrated in that zone and their properties (drainage, pH), without blaming whole-field weather as the differentiating factor.

results.answer:
The weak part is the southeast low‑productivity zone.  
It covers 22.4 % of the field (48.3 acres).  
Its NDVI is 0.769, lower than other zones.  
The zone contains Wehadkee silt loam (12.6 % of the zone).  
This soil is poorly drained.  
Poor drainage caused wet stress early in the season and limited rooting.  
The zone also contains Roanoke silt loam (40.7 %).  
This soil is poorly drained, has pH 4.5, and low available water.  
These conditions further reduced root growth.  
Augusta silt loam (32.1 %) is somewhat poorly drained and also has low pH.  
The combination of poor drainage and low pH explains the weak growth.

judge.detail: The answer corrects the rainfall to 27.9 inches, attributes the weakness to Bama fine sandy loam's low water holding capacity and pH rather than heat, and provides the USDA county yield figure.

results.answer:
The weak part is on the east side and covers 2.8 % of the field.  
Soil there is Bama fine sandy loam with pH 5.0 and water holding 5.7 in, below the field average 6.2 in.  
It dries out first in dry spells.  
Therefore the low zone is weaker because of low water and low pH, not because of heat.

Season rain was 27.9 in, not 40 in.  
County‑level yield estimate is 843 lb/acre, 80 % range 633‑1046 lb/acre.  
USDA reported 825 lb/acre, slightly below the model estimate.

Apply lime before next spring to raise the soil pH toward the optimal 6.0‑6.5 range.

Plant cotton in the late‑April through May window.  
Today is 3 Nov 2026, so planting must wait until the next season.
